sessions.description: This session addresses the 'Demandingness' objection: if we must always maximize utility, can we ever spend money on a movie or time on a hobby instead of saving lives? You will evaluate whether utilitarianism asks too much of human nature. This helps you reconcile high-level ethical theory with the practical realities of personal life.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the comfort of the classroom setting. The core issue of 'Demandingness' is that Utilitarianism, if taken seriously, doesn't just ask us to be 'nice'; it asks us to be saints. Begin by visualizing a scale on the whiteboard: on one side is the 'Utility of a $15 Movie Ticket' (transient personal pleasure) and on the other is the 'Utility of a Life-Saving Vaccine' (years of potential life). The logical problem for the Utilitarian is that there is no principled way to stop the scale from tilting toward the vaccine every single time. This introduces the 'Integrity' or 'Demandingness' objection: does a moral theory that requires us to give away everything until we are at the same level as the poorest person on Earth lose its authority by being psychologically impossible?

Introduce Peter Singer’s famous 'Pond' thought experiment as the primary engine for this argument. Explain that the logical chain starts with a simple premise: suffering and death from lack of food, shelter, and medical care are bad. If it is in our power to prevent something bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought, morally, to do it. On the whiteboard, draw the 'Drowning Child' next to the 'Luxury Purchase.' The key insight here is the removal of distance; Singer argues that in a globalized world, a child dying in another country is no different from the child in the pond right in front of us. This is the moment to watch for the common student misconception that 'charity is optional.' You must emphasize that for a Utilitarian, this isn't 'charity'—it is a strict moral obligation, as binding as the duty not to kill.

Transition to the 'Point of Marginal Utility.' This is the technical limit of the theory where giving more would cause as much suffering to the donor as it would relieve in the recipient. Draw a graph showing the diminishing returns of personal wealth versus the exponential growth of utility for the global poor. The 'Demandingness' objection arises here: if I cannot have a hobby, a special meal, or a career in the arts because those resources could save more lives elsewhere, do I still have a life of my own? Explain that critics argue Utilitarianism 'alienates' us from our own projects and commitments, effectively turning us into 'utility-producing machines' rather than autonomous agents.

To provide a balanced view, present the Utilitarian counter-arguments. One strategy is 'Rule Utilitarianism,' which suggests that a society that demands total self-sacrifice might collapse or lead to burnout, actually resulting in less total utility in the long run. Another response is 'The Incentive Argument': if we allow people to keep some wealth, they remain productive and can give more over a lifetime. Use the whiteboard to map these as 'Strategic Concessions' rather than 'Moral Permissions.' This helps the learner see that the theory can be pragmatic without losing its logical core. Conclude by asking the learner to identify a 'middle ground' threshold—this practice is designed to reveal whether they prioritize the internal consistency of the theory (the Singer approach) or the practical limits of human psychology.

tasks: Explain Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' argument briefly.
Discuss one possible utilitarian response to the demandingness objection.

sessions.title: Trolley Problems
sessions.description: This session uses the classic 'Trolley Problem' and its variations (Switch vs. Footbridge) as a diagnostic tool to map your moral intuitions. You will learn to use these thought experiments to isolate variables in ethical reasoning. Mastering these puzzles allows you to test the limits of consequentialism in a controlled, logical way.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the Trolley Problem not as a mere pop-culture meme, but as a high-precision laboratory for moral philosophy. The goal is to maximize well-being by stripping away the messy variables of real-world politics to isolate the core conflict between utility-based logic and moral 'gut' reactions. On the whiteboard, I will first draw the 'Switch' case: a runaway trolley headed for five people, with a lever that can divert it to a track with only one person. The core concept here is the 'calculus of aggregation.' Most students instinctively choose to pull the lever, demonstrating an implicit acceptance of the utilitarian principle that five lives outweigh one. This establishes the baseline for a consequentialist framework where the metric of success is the total sum of preserved human utility.

Next, we transition to the 'Footbridge' variation to challenge this consistency. In this diagram, the trolley is still heading for five people, but the only way to stop it is to push a large person off a bridge into its path. Logically, the outcome is identical to the Switch case: five live, one dies. However, the intuition usually flips. Here, I will emphasize the distinction between 'foreseeing' a death as a side effect and 'intending' a death as a direct means to an end. This is where we address the potential fallacy that ethics is just a math problem; if the learner feels a shift in their conviction despite the math remaining constant, we have successfully isolated a variable—physical agency and the violation of bodily integrity—that utilitarianism traditionally struggles to weigh properly.

To bridge the gap between these two cases, I will introduce the 'Loop' variant. This is a crucial intermediate step to prevent the misconception that the difference is simply about 'touching' someone. In the Loop case, the diverted track loops back to the five people, and the only thing stopping the trolley is the body of the one person on the side track. This forces the learner to confront whether they are using the one person merely as a tool. By visualizing these three scenarios side-by-side, we map a spectrum of moral permissibility. This process is essential because it forces the student to decide: is their 'Switch' intuition correct (making them a consistent utilitarian), or is their 'Footbridge' intuition the more reliable moral signal? 

We conclude with an active diagnostic exercise. I will ask the students to justify why they might treat the 'Switch' and 'Footbridge' differently. If they struggle to find a logical distinction, I will point out that this discomfort is the 'utility-rights' friction point. The most important takeaway is that if we prioritize the outcome above all else to maximize net happiness, we must be prepared to accept the Footbridge conclusion. If we cannot, we have discovered the limits of the utilitarian framework in our own reasoning. This session prepares them for the next by proving that while logic is a powerful tool for social benefit, it often operates in tension with deeply held human norms regarding individual sanctity.

tasks: Identify the difference between the 'Switch' case and the 'Footbridge' case from a utilitarian perspective.
Explain why many people have different intuitions about these two cases despite identical outcomes.

sessions.title: Moral Intuition as Evidence
sessions.description: This session concludes the unit by asking how much weight we should give to our 'gut feelings' when they contradict a logical principle like utilitarianism. You will revisit the concept of 'Reflective Equilibrium' from Unit 1 to see if we should revise our principles or our intuitions. This prepares you for the 'Moral Case Analysis' by providing a methodology for handling internal moral conflict.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by acknowledging the intellectual 'collision' we have been building toward throughout this unit: the moment where the cold, logical calculus of Utilitarianism meets the visceral, immediate scream of our moral intuition. In this whiteboard session, start by drawing two columns: one labeled 'Principles' and the other 'Intuitions.' Remind the student that Utilitarianism is a 'top-down' system that values consistency above all else. Ask them to reflect on the cases we've seen—the organ harvesting surgeon or the footbridge pusher. In these cases, our logical system (maximize life) and our gut feeling (don't kill an innocent) are in a dead heat. The central question of this session is not which one is 'right' in a vacuum, but how a rational person decides which one to sacrifice when they conflict.

Introduce the concept of 'Reflective Equilibrium' by drawing a double-headed arrow between the two columns. Explain that moral reasoning isn't a one-way street where principles dictate reality; rather, it is a process of back-and-forth adjustment. If a principle leads to an absolutely abhorrent conclusion (like the 'Sheriff and the Mob' case), we might need to revise the principle. Conversely, if our intuitions are based on mere prejudice or evolutionary baggage, we might need to discard the intuition in favor of the principle. The goal of this 'equilibrium' is to reach a state where our specific judgments and our general rules are in harmony. This prevents the student from falling into the trap of 'Moral Relativism'—where anything goes—or 'Fanaticism'—where the theory is followed blindly even into madness.

To sharpen this, visualize the 'Hierarchy of Evidence.' When should we trust our gut? Often, our moral intuitions act like sensory perceptions; they are 'moral data points.' However, just as an optical illusion can trick our eyes, our moral sense can be tricked by proximity or emotional bias. Use the contrast between the 'Switch' and 'Footbridge' trolley cases to illustrate this: why does our intuition change when we have to use our hands? Is that a meaningful moral difference, or just a psychological quirk? The most important takeaway here is for the student to identify 'noisy' intuitions—those triggered by fear or disgust—versus 'stable' intuitions—those that persist even after calm reflection.

End the session by setting up a 'Conflict Resolution' flowchart on the board. When an intuition and a principle clash, the student should ask: Does the principle have a strong logical justification? (e.g., fairness, well-being). Does the intuition survive a 'sanity check' across different contexts? If the answer to both is yes, they are in a state of productive tension. Use the practice tasks to have the student actively choose sides in a hypothetical. In the first task, look for them to defend a principle (like honesty) even when it hurts feelings; in the second, look for them to defend an intuition (like saving a family member over two strangers) even when it violates pure utility. This prepares them for the Moral Case Analysis by teaching them that 'solving' an ethical dilemma isn't about finding a math answer, but about justifying which part of their moral compass they are choosing to prioritize.

tasks: Describe a situation where you would choose to trust a principle over an intuition.
Describe a situation where you would choose to trust an intuition over a principle.

projects.stage_description: Apply consequentialist reasoning to your chosen case by identifying stakeholders and predicting outcomes to determine the 'greatest happiness.'
projects.deliverable_increment: A 'Consequentialist Impact Report' that calculates potential hedonic outcomes and addresses the tension between aggregate good and individual rights.

exams.title: Consequences Unit Exam
exams.goal: Assess the learner's ability to apply utilitarian principles, distinguish between different theories of the good, and respond to common objections with philosophical rigor.
sections: Comprehensive evaluation covering the Greatest Happiness Principle, Act vs. Rule Utilitarianism, theories of well-being (Hedonism and Preference), and major objections including rights, demandingness, and trolley problems.
successCriteria: Correctly identify act vs. rule utilitarian approaches in varied scenarios.
Explain the 'Experience Machine' argument and its implications for hedonism.
Articulate why utilitarianism is often accused of failing to respect individual rights.
Apply aggregate utility calculations to a policy-based case study.

units.title: Duties and Rights
units.description: Investigate deontological ethics through Kantian duty, the philosophy of rights, and competing theories of distributive justice.

lectures.title: Kantian Ethics
lectures.description: This lecture explores Immanuel Kant's revolutionary deontological framework, shifting the focus from the consequences of actions to the inherent duty and rationality behind them.

sessions.title: The Good Will
sessions.description: This session introduces the foundational Kantian concept that only a 'good will'—acting out of duty rather than inclination—is unconditionally good. You will learn to distinguish between acting in conformity with duty and acting from the motive of duty, which is essential for understanding the moral worth of an agent in a non-consequentialist framework.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common intuition that morality is about the outcome of our actions. In a public-lecture style, draw a sharp contrast with the Utilitarian framework discussed previously. On the whiteboard, write the phrase 'Unconditional Good' and ask the audience to suggest candidates like happiness, intelligence, or courage. One by one, debunk these by showing how they can be used for evil—a clever criminal or a courageous villain. This leads to the fundamental Kantian claim: the only thing that is good without qualification is a 'Good Will.' Explain that for Kant, the moral worth of an action doesn't reside in what it achieves, but in the principle or 'maxim' that motivates the agent.

To make this abstract concept concrete, use the whiteboard to map out the distinction between 'Acting in Conformity with Duty' and 'Acting from Duty.' Use the classic example of the Honest Shopkeeper. Draw two columns. In the first, the shopkeeper is honest because it is good for business (prudence/inclination); in the second, the shopkeeper is honest because honesty is a moral requirement (duty). Emphasize that while the external behavior is identical, only the second shopkeeper possesses moral worth in Kant's eyes. This is a crucial pivot: students often struggle with the idea that 'doing the right thing' isn't enough—the reason 'why' you do it is the engine of ethics.

Introduce a more provocative example to test the limits of this theory: the Sympathetic Helper vs. the Grumpy Helper. Contrast someone who helps others because they naturally enjoy doing so (inclination) with someone who feels no cold-heartedness but helps simply because they recognize it is their duty. Explicitly address the common misconception that Kant 'hates' emotions; explain that he doesn't think it's bad to feel sympathy, but he argues that sympathy is a fickle, unreliable basis for morality. The core pedagogical goal here is to show that a Good Will is autonomous—it doesn't depend on how we happen to feel on a given day.

Conclude the session with a reflective exercise where the learner must categorize motives in various scenarios. Ask them to identify if a person helping a neighbor to get a tax break, or because they feel pity, or because it's 'the right thing to do,' possesses moral worth. This exercise is designed to reveal the learner's own lingering consequentialist biases. Wrap up by reinforcing that the Good Will is the 'jewelry' of the moral life—it shines by its own light even if the agent is unable to actually accomplish their goals due to bad luck. This sets the stage for the next session on how we actually determine what our duty is through the Categorical Imperative.

tasks: Identify the motive in three distinct scenarios: a shopkeeper being honest for profit, a person helping out of pity, and a person helping because it is right.
Explain why Kant believes happiness or intelligence are not 'unconditionally' good.

sessions.title: The Categorical Imperative
sessions.description: This session covers the First Formulation of the Categorical Imperative: the Formula of Universal Law. You will learn the procedural steps of the 'universalizability test' to determine if a maxim is morally permissible, providing you with a rigorous logical tool to evaluate moral rules without relying on emotional outcomes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing a fundamental distinction that separates Kantian ethics from almost every other form of practical reasoning: the difference between Hypothetical and Categorical Imperatives. I will draw two columns on the board. The first, 'Hypothetical,' represents 'if-then' statements—commands that only apply if you happen to want a specific outcome, like 'If you want to be healthy, eat vegetables.' I need to emphasize that these are not moral laws because they are optional. The second column, 'Categorical,' is where the moral weight lies. These are commands that apply to you simply because you are a rational agent, regardless of your desires. The core takeaway here is that morality isn't a suggestion for achieving happiness; it is a structural requirement of reason itself.

Next, I will introduce the 'Formula of Universal Law,' which serves as the diagnostic test for this categorical necessity. I'll write the famous line: 'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' It is vital to pause here and define a 'maxim'—not as a slogan, but as a personal rule of action (e.g., 'I will do X, in circumstances Y, for purpose Z'). Students often confuse this with the Golden Rule ('Do unto others...'), so I must clarify that Kant isn't asking how you would feel if someone did this to you; he is asking if the very idea of everyone doing it is logically coherent. We are looking for logical contradictions, not emotional discomfort.

To make this abstract principle concrete, I will lead the class through the 'Four-Step Universalizability Test' using the classic example of the 'Lying Promise.' On the board, I will map the progression: 1) Formulate the maxim ('I will make a false promise to get money I need'); 2) Universalize it ('Everyone makes false promises when they need money'); 3) Check for a contradiction in conception; and 4) Check for a contradiction in the will. I will highlight the 'Contradiction in Conception' as the most critical moment. If everyone makes false promises, the very institution of 'promising' collapses—no one would believe a promise anymore. Therefore, the action is logically impossible in a world where it is a universal law. This reveals that the person making the lying promise is trying to make an 'exception for themselves,' which is the hallmark of immorality for Kant.

Finally, I will address the common pitfall where students think Kant is worried about the bad consequences of a world full of liars. I must steer them back to the logic: it’s not that the world would be 'unpleasant,' but that the maxim would 'undermine itself.' To reinforce this, we will engage in a practice task where learners must differentiate between a command of skill (Hypothetical) and a command of morality (Categorical). By forcing them to identify why a specific maxim fails the test, they will see that Kantian ethics is about consistency and the rejection of the 'special pleader' status. This session transforms morality from a vague feeling into a rigorous, logical audit of our own intentions.

tasks: Formulate a maxim for 'making a lying promise' and run it through the four steps of the universalizability test.
Contrast a hypothetical imperative with a categorical imperative using specific examples.

sessions.title: Humanity as an End
sessions.description: This session focuses on the Second Formulation of the Categorical Imperative, which prohibits using humans merely as a means to an end. You will explore what it means to respect the rational nature of persons, which serves as a critical bridge between abstract logic and the practical treatment of individuals in ethical conflicts.
sessions.sessionOutline:
The core of today's session moves from the abstract logic of universal laws to the concrete moral status of the individual. We begin by introducing the Second Formulation of the Categorical Imperative: the Formula of Humanity. The central idea to communicate is that human beings, as rational agents capable of setting their own ends, possess a value that is absolute rather than relative. On the whiteboard, we draw a sharp distinction between 'objects' and 'persons.' Objects have 'price' (their value is derived from their use-value to someone else), while persons have 'dignity' (their value is intrinsic). This distinction is the bedrock for everything that follows, as it explains why Kantian ethics is inherently protective of individual rights against the 'greater good' arguments we encountered in Utilitarianism.

We must then navigate the nuance of the word 'merely.' A common student misconception is that Kant prohibits using people as a means at all, which would make everyday life—like hiring a plumber or buying groceries—immoral. I will explicitly address this by writing 'Treating as a Means' vs. 'Treating MERELY as a Means' on the board. We use the plumber example to show that as long as there is mutual consent and the plumber's agency is respected (they are not coerced or deceived), we are using their services while still respecting them as an end. The violation occurs when we bypass a person's capacity to consent, effectively turning them into a tool for our own purposes. This is the moment to introduce the concept of 'in principle' consent: Could the other person, in principle, agree to the action if they knew all the facts?

To put this into practice, we shift to a workplace automation scenario. We'll sketch out a flowchart where a company replaces staff with AI. If the transition is done through deception or by treating workers as disposable components to be discarded without regard for their agency, it fails the Kantian test. We use this to reveal that the ethical failure isn't the use of technology itself, but the 'thing-ification' of the employees. This exercise helps students realize that Kantian ethics provides a robust language for labor rights and corporate responsibility that goes beyond just calculating severance pay.

Finally, we engage in a direct head-to-head comparison between Utilitarianism and Deontology using a 'Trolley-style' variant, such as the Transplant Case (killing one healthy person to save five). While a Utilitarian might struggle with the 'math' of the situation, the Kantian answer is a hard 'No.' By visualizing the one person on the board as a 'Rational End-in-Themselves,' we demonstrate that their life cannot be 'spent' to purchase the lives of others. This comparison is vital because it reveals the 'bridge' mentioned in the session goals: the Formula of Humanity is what gives us the 'side-constraints' that prevent individuals from being sacrificed for the collective. We conclude by emphasizing that for Kant, the morality of an action is found in how it treats the humanity of the person in front of us, regardless of the global outcome.

tasks: Analyze a workplace scenario involving automation to determine if employees are being treated 'merely as a means'.
Compare how a Utilitarian and a Kantian would approach the use of a single person to save five others.

sessions.title: Autonomy and Dignity
sessions.description: This session examines the Kantian concepts of autonomy and the 'Kingdom of Ends,' where individuals are both authors and subjects of moral law. You will understand how dignity arises from our capacity for self-legislation, providing a philosophical foundation for the modern concept of human rights and personal agency.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this final session on Kantian ethics, we move from the mechanical application of the Categorical Imperative to the majestic 'why'—the ultimate status of the human person. The session begins by contrasting the concept of Autonomy with Heteronomy. On the whiteboard, draw a circle representing the 'Self.' Illustrate Heteronomy as external arrows—desires, social pressure, biology, or divine command—pushing the self to act. Explain that if we act only to satisfy a craving or to obey an external law, we are not truly free; we are merely complex biological machines reacting to stimuli. The core insight here is that for Kant, freedom isn't the ability to do whatever you want; it is the ability to give a law to yourself through reason. This 'Self-Legislation' is the definition of Autonomy, and it is the only source of moral worth.

Transition to the concept of Dignity by connecting it to this capacity for autonomy. On the whiteboard, create a distinction between 'Price' and 'Dignity.' Explain that things with a price are replaceable—one iPhone can be swapped for another of equal value. However, a rational being who can choose their own ends has 'Dignity,' which is an intrinsic, incomparable value. This explains why we cannot 'trade' one person to save five; to do so treats a being with dignity as if they merely had a price. The most common pitfall for students here is confusing Kantian autonomy with modern individualism or 'doing your own thing.' You must clarify that we are autonomous only when we follow the universal moral law that reason reveals to us, not when we follow our subjective whims.

Introduce the 'Kingdom of Ends' as the grand synthesis of these ideas. Ask the learner to imagine a society where every individual is both a 'Sovereign' (making the laws via their reason) and a 'Subject' (obeying those same laws). This is a thought experiment in social organization: a community where no one is treated as a tool and everyone respects the autonomy of others. This is the philosophical bedrock of modern human rights. On the board, map out how the Categorical Imperative (the rule) leads to the respect for Humanity (the value), which culminates in the Kingdom of Ends (the ideal society). This visualization helps the learner see Kant's project not just as a set of rigid 'don'ts,' but as a visionary blueprint for a world of mutual respect.

Conclude with a practice moment centered on 'Heteronomy.' Provide a scenario where someone does the right thing—say, donating to charity—but does it only because they fear social shaming or want a tax break. Ask the learner to identify the heteronomous force at play. This reveals whether the learner understands that for Kant, the 'why' (the autonomy of the will) is what generates the 'dignity' of the act. Finally, reflect on the 'Kingdom of Ends' as a diagnostic tool for modern institutions. If a workplace or a government treats people as mere cogs, it fails the ideal of the Kingdom of Ends. This bridges the gap between 18th-century metaphysics and contemporary political and professional ethics.

tasks: Define 'heteronomy' and provide an example of an action governed by heteronomous forces.
Explain how the concept of a 'Kingdom of Ends' functions as an ideal for social organization.

lectures.title: Rights
lectures.description: This lecture examines the nature and function of rights as moral 'trump cards' that protect individuals from being sacrificed for the greater good.

sessions.title: What Rights Are
sessions.description: This session defines the concept of moral and legal rights, exploring Wesley Hohfeld's analysis of claims, privileges, powers, and immunities. You will be able to identify what a right-holder is entitled to and who bears the corresponding duty, clarifying the structure of moral claims in social disagreements.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by clarifying that while everyone uses the word 'rights' in daily conversation, few can define what a right actually is beyond a vague feeling of entitlement. The goal of this session is to move from that fuzzy intuition to a rigorous analytical framework. Explain that rights act as 'moral shields'—they are constraints on how others can treat us, regardless of whether it would benefit the majority to ignore them. Use the visual metaphor of a 'No Trespassing' sign to represent the boundary of a right-holder’s moral domain.

Introduce the fundamental distinction between Moral Rights and Legal Rights. A moral right exists independently of whether a government recognizes it (like the right not to be tortured), whereas a legal right is a specific entitlement codified in a system (like the right to a 30-day return policy). To prevent the common misconception that 'all rights are just laws,' use the counter-example of a whistleblower in an authoritarian regime: they have a moral right to speak the truth even if their legal rights are being violated. This demonstrates that rights can serve as a benchmark for criticizing laws.

Transition to the core technical framework: Wesley Hohfeld’s analysis of rights. On the whiteboard, draw a clear link between a 'Claim Right' and a 'Duty.' Explain that a right for person A is meaningless unless it creates a specific obligation for person B. For example, if I own a piece of property, my 'claim right' to exclusive use is essentially the 'duty' of everyone else to stay off it. This is the 'Jural Correlative'—the idea that every right is a two-way street. If there is no one who has a duty to provide or refrain, the 'right' is merely an empty wish.

Expand the whiteboard map to include 'Privileges' (or Liberties). Contrast this with a claim: a privilege means you have no duty *not* to do something, but it doesn't necessarily mean others have a duty to help you. Use the example of a public park: you have a privilege to walk there, but you don't have a claim right to stop others from walking there too. This distinction helps learners understand that not all freedoms are protected from interference in the same way.

Introduce 'Powers' and 'Immunities' to complete the Hohfeldian square. A Power is the ability to change someone else's legal or moral status—like the power of a judge to issue a ruling or an owner to sell property. An Immunity is a protection against someone else’s power—like the First Amendment protecting a citizen from the government's power to censor. This prevents the mistake of treating rights as static objects; instead, students should see them as dynamic relationships of authority.

Conclude by having the learner map a real-world scenario—such as intellectual property—using these terms. Ask them to identify exactly who holds the 'claim' and what 'duty' the rest of the world owes them. This practice reveals whether the learner understands that rights are not just 'things' we have, but 'logical relations' between persons. This analytical clarity is the prerequisite for the next sessions on positive vs. negative rights.

tasks: Map out the relationship between a 'claim right' and a 'duty' using a property ownership example.
Differentiate between a moral right and a legal right with a specific counter-example.

sessions.title: Negative and Positive Rights
sessions.description: This session distinguishes between negative rights (rights to non-interference) and positive rights (rights to assistance). You will learn to categorize common rights like free speech or healthcare, which is vital for understanding the political and economic implications of different ethical stances.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by positioning this session as a critical taxonomy for modern political and ethical debate. We move from the formal definition of 'rights' established in the previous session to the substantive distinction between what we are owed in terms of 'omission' versus 'provision.' Use the whiteboard to draw a line down the center, labeling one side 'Negative' and the other 'Positive.' Explain that this distinction is primarily about the nature of the duty-bearer’s obligation: is the world required to leave you alone, or is it required to step in and help you?

Begin the exploration of Negative Rights by framing them as 'Freedom From.' Use the example of free speech or bodily integrity. On the whiteboard, illustrate this as a protective 'bubble' around the individual. The key logic to convey is that for a negative right to be respected, the rest of the world effectively has to do 'nothing.' This is why they are often associated with classical liberalism; they are conceptually 'cheap' in that they don't require active resource redistribution. However, challenge the learners by pointing out a common misconception: even negative rights require positive enforcement. A right to property (negative) is meaningless without a taxpayer-funded police force (positive action) to protect it. This nuance prevents the learner from oversimplifying negative rights as purely 'passive' in practice.

Transition to Positive Rights by framing them as 'Entitlements To.' Use the examples of healthcare or clean water. On the whiteboard, draw an arrow pointing from society into the individual’s bubble. Explain that these rights imply a claim on the labor, resources, or time of others. The core philosophical tension here is the 'source of the duty.' If I have a right to a doctor, does that mean the doctor is a slave to my right? Of course not, but it does mean the state or the collective has a duty to facilitate that access. This leads into the first practice task: asking students to classify complex cases like the 'right to a fair trial.' Students often struggle here because a fair trial requires the state to *not* convict you unfairly (negative) but also requires the state to *provide* a judge and a public defender (positive). The goal of this exercise is to show that most real-world rights are 'clusters' rather than pure types.

Deepen the analysis by addressing the libertarian critique that 'positive rights are not real rights.' This is the most important argumentative hurdle in the session. Use the whiteboard to map the logical chain: if a positive right requires resources, and resources come from taxation, then a positive right to healthcare necessarily involves a violation of a negative right to property. Ask the learners to weigh this trade-off. This sets up the second practice task: arguing for or against the claim that positive rights are inherently 'parasitic' on negative rights. The instructor should guide this not toward a 'correct' political answer, but toward an analytical understanding of how different ethical frameworks prioritize these claims. For instance, a Utilitarian might see the positive right to water as overriding a negative right to wealth, whereas a strict Deontologist might see the violation of the negative right as an impermissible use of a person as a mere means.

Conclude by connecting these categories back to the broader theme of human dignity. Explain that the distinction between negative and positive rights determines the 'size' of the government and the 'scope' of our moral obligations to strangers. By the end of the session, the whiteboard should clearly reflect that while negative rights protect our 'liberty,' positive rights aim to ensure our 'well-being,' and the friction between the two is the engine of most modern legal and moral conflicts.

tasks: Classify the following as positive or negative: the right to life, the right to a fair trial, the right to clean water.
Argue for or against the claim that every positive right requires a negative right to be violated.

sessions.title: Conflicts of Rights
sessions.description: This session tackles the difficult problem of what happens when two valid rights clash, such as the right to privacy versus the right to security. You will learn about hierarchy and specification theories of rights, giving you a framework to resolve complex civil liberties issues.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by acknowledging a conceptual crisis: in the previous sessions, we treated rights as absolute moral boundaries, but in the real world, rights frequently collide. To illustrate this, draw a horizontal line on the board representing a 'Right to Free Speech' and a crossing vertical line representing a 'Right to Physical Safety.' The intersection point is where the theory breaks down. The core goal of this session is to move beyond the simplistic view that rights are binary 'on/off' switches and instead provide a structural method for navigating these intersections.

Introduce the 'Specification' approach as the first strategy. On the whiteboard, visualize this as a 'sculpting' process. Rather than saying rights have exceptions, specificationists argue that rights are just highly defined from the start. For example, instead of a general 'Right to Free Speech' that is later balanced against safety, we redefine the right as 'The Right to Speak Freely Provided One Does Not Incite Immediate Violence.' Explain to the learner that this solves the conflict by 'drawing the lines' so they never actually touch. The importance of this idea lies in its precision; it maintains the 'trump card' status of rights by ensuring that a properly defined right is never actually overridden—it just doesn't apply to the conflicting case.

Transition to the second strategy: W.D. Ross’s concept of 'Prima Facie' rights. If specification is like sculpting, Ross’s approach is like a courtroom scale. Use the whiteboard to list 'Prima Facie' (at first glance) duties and rights versus 'Actual' duties. Teach the learner that we have a standing moral obligation to respect privacy and a standing obligation to ensure security. When they clash, we must determine which duty is more 'stringent' in that specific context. This is a critical pivot because it admits that rights can be 'outweighed' without being 'violated.' A common pitfall for students is thinking that if a right is outweighed, it wasn't a real right. Use the example of breaking into a cabin to escape a blizzard; the owner's property right is outweighed by your right to life, but you still owe them for the broken door—this 'moral residue' proves the right still exists even when it loses the conflict.

Engage the learner in a practice exercise regarding hate speech. On the board, create a T-chart. On one side, list the components of the 'Right to Expression'; on the other, the 'Right to be Free from Harassment.' Ask the learner to apply the specification method: how would we rewrite the 'Right to Free Speech' to exclude specific harms without making the right meaningless? This reveals the difficulty of the 'slippery slope'—if we specify too much, the right disappears; if we specify too little, it becomes a weapon of harm. The key takeaway is that specification requires a deep commitment to defining the 'core' of a right versus its 'periphery.'

Conclude by mapping a hierarchy of rights. Draw a pyramid on the board, placing basic bodily integrity at the base and more abstract rights, like property or convenience, higher up. Explain that while there is no universally agreed-upon hierarchy, most ethical frameworks prioritize rights that are necessary for the exercise of all other rights (like life and agency). This hierarchy provides the 'tie-breaker' in Ross’s prima facie model. Summarize by emphasizing that resolving conflicts isn't about ignoring rights, but about honoring the most fundamental claims when we are forced to choose, ensuring the learner leaves with a toolkit for systemic moral weighing.

tasks: Apply a 'specification' approach to a case involving hate speech versus the right to safety.
Explain the concept of 'prima facie' rights as proposed by W.D. Ross.

sessions.title: Rights and Consequences
sessions.description: This session explores the tension between rights-based (deontological) and outcome-based (consequentialist) ethics. You will analyze Ronald Dworkin's idea of rights as 'trumps' and evaluate when, if ever, a right can be overridden for the sake of the collective good.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by positioning this session as the climax of the Rights lecture, where the theoretical definitions of the previous sessions meet the cold reality of trade-offs. The central metaphor for the whiteboard should be Ronald Dworkin’s concept of 'Rights as Trumps.' Visualize a card game on the board: on one side, you have 'Collective Goods' or 'Aggregate Utility' (represented by a stack of coins or points), and on the other, an individual’s 'Right' (represented by a trump card). Explain that if a right is a true moral entitlement, it cannot be defeated simply because the community would be slightly better off by ignoring it. This prevents the learner from falling into the trap of thinking rights are just 'really strong suggestions'—they are structural limits on what a majority or a government can do to a person.

Transition to the 'Ticking Time Bomb' scenario to test the limits of this 'Trump' logic. On the whiteboard, draw a scale: on one side, the life of one suspect; on the other, the lives of thousands of civilians. A pure utilitarian would see this as a simple math problem, but the rights-based theorist (Deontologist) must hold firm. Explain that from a strict rights perspective, the suspect's right against torture is non-negotiable because violating it treats the human being as a mere tool to achieve an end. Use this moment to point out a common learner misconception: that 'being ethical' always means 'saving the most lives.' Challenge them to see that if we allow rights to be calculated away in emergencies, the very definition of a 'right' disappears. The goal here is to make the learner feel the discomfort of the 'clean hands' versus 'dirty hands' dilemma.

Now, pivot to the Utilitarian perspective, but in a more nuanced way than simple calculation. Introduce the concept of 'Rule Utilitarianism' or the 'Instrumental Value' of rights. On the board, map out how a Utilitarian might actually defend rights—not because they are sacred, but because a society that respects rights (like the right to property or free speech) is generally more stable and prosperous in the long run. Contrast this with Dworkin: for Dworkin, the right is valuable in itself; for the Utilitarian, the right is a useful policy. This distinction is crucial because it explains why a Utilitarian might support a right right up until the moment it becomes catastrophic to do so, whereas the Rights-theorist stays the course.

Conclude by revisiting the tension between individual dignity and the common good. Use the whiteboard to create a 'Moral Map' that summarizes the lecture: place Dworkin and Kant on one side (Individual Priority) and Bentham/Mill on the other (Collective Priority). Ask the learner to identify where they would 'draw the line' if the stakes were not a bomb, but something more mundane like eminent domain or public health mandates. This final reflection task is designed to reveal if the learner can now articulate the difference between a right being 'absolute' versus 'prima facie.' The takeaway should be that while rights protect us from the 'tyranny of the majority,' the cost of that protection is often a loss in total social efficiency.

tasks: Draft a short response to the 'Ticking Time Bomb' scenario from a strict rights-based perspective.
Identify a situation where a Utilitarian might support a right for purely instrumental reasons.

lectures.title: Justice
lectures.description: This lecture transitions from individual duties and rights to the broader question of how a society should distribute its benefits and burdens fairly.

sessions.title: Distributive Justice
sessions.description: This session introduces the core question of distributive justice: how should wealth, opportunity, and power be allocated? You will learn about different patterns of distribution (equality, merit, need), setting the stage for evaluating the fairness of economic systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a large circle on the whiteboard, representing the total 'Social Pie'—the wealth, opportunities, and honors of a society. The goal is to move the student from thinking about justice as simple 'punishment' to 'distribution.' Explain that while Unit 3 has focused on individual rights, we are now asking how a collective body fairly divides the benefits and burdens of cooperation. Avoid technical jargon initially; instead, ask the learner to imagine a group project where one person did 80% of the work, one provided the resources, and one just joined at the end. Use this to frame the central question: what does 'fairness' actually look like when the pie is finite?

Introduce the concept of 'Strict Equality' by drawing equal slices in the pie. The primary logic here is the inherent moral equality of persons. However, immediately challenge this by introducing the 'Merit' counter-point. On the board, create a contrast table between 'Equality of Outcome' and 'Equality of Opportunity.' The critical insight for the learner is that treating people exactly the same can sometimes feel profoundly unjust if their efforts or needs differ wildly. This helps them see that distributive justice isn't just about math; it's about which human values we choose to prioritize.

Transition to the three primary categories of 'Social Goods' that are subject to distribution: Wealth (economic), Opportunity (education/jobs), and Power (political influence). Use a flowchart to show how these goods interact—for example, how an unfair distribution of education leads to an unfair distribution of wealth. This is a crucial moment to address a common misconception: that distributive justice is only about money. By widening the scope to include 'power' and 'burdens' (like taxes or military service), the student begins to see the structural nature of society as a designed system rather than a random collection of individuals.

End the session with a 'merit vs. need' diagnostic exercise. Present a scenario of a limited supply of a life-saving drug. Should it go to the person who can pay the most (market merit), the person who discovered it (intellectual merit), or the person who is sickest (need)? Draw these as competing paths on the whiteboard. This exercise is designed to reveal the learner's own intuitive 'starting point' for justice, which prepares them for the more formal theories of Rawls and Nozick in the upcoming sessions. Emphasize that there is no 'neutral' distribution; every system reflects an underlying ethical choice.

tasks: Compare the 'strictly equal' distribution of a resource with a 'merit-based' distribution in a specific workplace context.
List three 'social goods' that are subject to distributive justice.

sessions.title: Rawls and the Original Position
sessions.description: This session covers John Rawls's 'Justice as Fairness,' including the Veil of Ignorance and the Difference Principle. You will use the thought experiment of the 'Original Position' to derive principles of justice that do not favor any particular social group, a cornerstone of modern liberal political philosophy.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the lecture by framing the fundamental problem John Rawls addresses: how can we agree on the rules of society when our personal biases—our wealth, gender, race, or talents—always cloud our judgment? To ground this, use the whiteboard to draw a simple 'Bargaining Table' where different people (a billionaire, a homeless person, a doctor) are trying to write a constitution. The visual takeaway should be the inherent conflict of interest. Explain that Rawls’s brilliance lies in moving from 'what is fair' to 'what would we agree to if we didn't know who we were?' Introduce the concept of 'Justice as Fairness' as the result of a fair procedure, rather than a pre-defined outcome.

Introduce the 'Original Position' and the 'Veil of Ignorance' as a cognitive filter. On the whiteboard, draw a thick vertical line representing the Veil. On the left side, list 'Personal Identity' (talents, social class, religion, gender); on the right side, show only 'Rational Agents' who have general knowledge of psychology and economics but zero knowledge of their own place in the world. Emphasize that this is not a historical event but a thought experiment designed to ensure impartiality. The logic here is critical: if you don’t know if you’ll be a star athlete or someone with a chronic disability, you won't vote for a system that leaves the disabled to starve.

Guide the learner through the 'Maximin' reasoning strategy—maximizing the minimum position. Ask the learner to design a healthcare system from behind the veil. The goal of this exercise is to reveal that rational agents are 'risk-averse' when the stakes are their entire lives. They won't choose a utilitarian system that sacrifices 5% of the population for the luxury of the rest, because they might be part of that 5%. This leads directly into the 'First Principle': Equal Basic Liberties. Use the whiteboard to list these (speech, conscience, assembly), explaining that no economic gain can justify trading away these fundamental rights.

Transition to the 'Difference Principle' to address the inevitable economic inequalities. This is often a point of confusion; students often mistake it for pure communism. Clarify that Rawls allows for inequality—like paying doctors more—but only if that inequality makes the person at the bottom better off than they would be under strict equality. Draw two bar charts: one with equal but low wealth for everyone, and one with unequal but higher 'floor' wealth for the poorest. Explain that the latter is 'more just' according to Rawls because it benefits the least advantaged through incentives and productivity.

Conclude by addressing the 'Fair Equality of Opportunity' principle, which acts as a bridge. It’s not enough that the Difference Principle helps the poor; the path to the high-paying jobs must be open to everyone regardless of their starting point in life. Use the whiteboard to synthesize the two principles into a hierarchy: Liberty first, then Fair Opportunity, then the Difference Principle. This hierarchy prevents the 'Just Society' from becoming a benevolent tyranny where wealth is high but freedom is low. This preparation sets the stage for the next session, where Nozick will challenge the very idea that we have the right to redistribute this wealth at all.

tasks: Perform a 'Veil of Ignorance' exercise regarding the design of a healthcare system.
State the Difference Principle and explain how it allows for inequality only if it benefits the least advantaged.

sessions.title: Libertarianism
sessions.description: This session presents Robert Nozick's entitlement theory of justice, focusing on historical justice and self-ownership. You will learn to critique patterned theories of justice (like Rawls's) from a perspective that prioritizes individual liberty and property rights, forming a sharp contrast to egalitarian views.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by contrasting the 'institutional' view of justice we saw in Rawls with a 'historical' view. On the whiteboard, draw a distinction between 'End-State' principles (how the pie looks right now) and 'Historical' principles (how the pie was made). Explain that for Robert Nozick, justice isn't about whether the final distribution of wealth looks 'fair' or 'equal' by a certain pattern; it’s about whether the process of acquiring and transferring property was clean. This shifts the focus from social engineering to individual rights, specifically the concept of 'Self-Ownership.' If I own my body, I own my labor, and by extension, I own the fruits of that labor. This logic serves as the bedrock for the Libertarian critique of any distributive scheme that requires constant state intervention.

Introduce the centerpiece of Nozick’s argument: the 'Wilt Chamberlain' thought experiment. On the board, set up 'D1,' an initial distribution where everyone has an equal amount of money. Then, describe a scenario where one million people voluntarily pay twenty-five cents extra to watch Wilt Chamberlain play basketball. At the end of the season, Wilt has $250,000, and everyone else has slightly less. Ask the learner: 'Is this new distribution (D2) unjust?' The key takeaway is that if D1 was just, and the transition to D2 happened through purely voluntary exchanges, then D2 must also be just. This demonstrates that 'liberty upsets patterns.' Any attempt to maintain a specific pattern (like Rawls’s Difference Principle) would require the state to constantly interfere with people’s lives to stop them from spending their money how they want.

Address a common misconception: that Libertarianism is just 'greed.' Clarify that Nozick’s Entitlement Theory has three strict components: Justice in Acquisition (taking something from nature that isn't owned), Justice in Transfer (voluntary trade/gift), and Rectification. Use the whiteboard to map out a 'chain of title.' If a piece of land was stolen three generations ago, the current 'owner' does not have a just title to it, even if they bought it honestly. This is 'Rectificatory Justice.' It is a crucial nuance because it shows that Libertarians aren't necessarily defending the current status quo if that status quo is built on historical theft or coercion.

Transition to the most provocative part of the lecture: the comparison between taxation and forced labor. Explain Nozick’s argument that if the state takes a percentage of your earnings, they are essentially taking a percentage of your time—the hours you worked to earn that money. Visually represent this as a 'time-theft' equation. This forces the learner to confront whether the 'social good' (like funding a hospital) justifies treating an individual as a means to an end. It challenges the collectivist 'we' by asserting that there is no social entity, only individual people with their own separate lives.

Conclude by setting up a comparative task. Ask the learner to take a specific scenario—for example, a billionaire who earned their money through a tech startup—and analyze it through both the Rawlsian and Nozickian lenses. The goal of this exercise is to show that the disagreement isn't usually about the math of the distribution, but about the fundamental starting point: Do we start with a collective 'pot' of resources to be divided, or do we start with individual rights that cannot be violated even for the sake of the 'least advantaged'?

tasks: Explain the 'Wilt Chamberlain' argument and how it purports to show that 'liberty upsets patterns'.
Distinguish between 'rectificatory justice' and 'distributive justice' in Nozick’s framework.

sessions.title: Egalitarian Responses
sessions.description: This session evaluates the debate between Rawls and his critics, including Luck Egalitarianism and the Capability Approach. You will learn to synthesize these views to address real-world inequality, preparing you to apply a sophisticated lens of justice to your final project case.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing a subtle tension left hanging from our discussion of Rawls and Nozick: if we agree that fairness matters, what exactly are we trying to equalize? This session moves beyond simple income redistribution to explore the more nuanced terrain of 'Luck Egalitarianism.' I will start by drawing a conceptual line on the board between 'Option Luck'—the results of calculated risks like gambling or investing—and 'Brute Luck'—factors like genetic health or being born into a war zone. The core teaching goal here is to help the learner see that while Rawls focused on the 'Basic Structure,' Luck Egalitarians like Ronald Dworkin want to go deeper, arguing that justice requires us to neutralize the effects of cosmic accidents while still holding individuals responsible for their choices. This prevents the common misconception that egalitarians want everyone to have the exact same outcome regardless of effort.

Next, I will introduce the 'Capability Approach' championed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum as a direct critique of 'Resource Egalitarianism.' On the whiteboard, I will contrast two individuals: one who is able-bodied and one who uses a wheelchair, both given the exact same bicycle. If we only look at resources (the bike), they are equal; however, if we look at 'functionings'—the actual ability to move around—they are not. The central insight for the learner is that justice isn't about the stuff we have, but what that stuff allows us to do and be. This shifts our focus from bank accounts to human flourishing, providing a much more sophisticated lens for the learner's final project analysis, especially when dealing with systemic inequalities that money alone cannot fix.

To bridge these theories, I will lead a brief mental exercise where I ask the learner to identify a 'brute luck' disadvantage in a contemporary setting, such as a chronic learning disability or being born into a zip code with failing infrastructure. I will prompt them to articulate why a purely Nozickian view might find this acceptable, versus why a Capability theorist would demand societal intervention. The aim is to reveal how our definition of 'equality' dictates our policy prescriptions: are we compensating for bad luck, or are we empowering human potential? This distinction is vital for preventing the 'victimhood trap'—the idea that egalitarianism is merely about handouts—and instead framing it as a quest for genuine agency.

Finally, I will conclude the session by synthesizing these responses into a 'Justice Toolkit.' I will map out how the learner can now look at a real-world case of inequality and ask three diagnostic questions: First, is this inequality a result of choice or luck? Second, are resources being distributed, or are capabilities being fostered? And third, does the current system prioritize property rights over the basic ability of citizens to function? This prepares the learner for the cumulative project by providing a structured, multi-dimensional framework that moves beyond the binary of 'Rawls vs. Nozick' and into the contemporary reality of social justice discourse.

tasks: Summarize the 'Capability Approach' as an alternative to focusing solely on income distribution.
Identify a 'brute luck' disadvantage and explain how an egalitarian might argue society should compensate for it.

projects.stage_description: Re-examine your case through a Kantian lens, testing the maxims of the involved parties for universalizability and respect for persons.
projects.deliverable_increment: A 'Deontological Review' section that evaluates the case based on duties, rights, and the principle of humanity.

exams.title: Duties and Rights Comprehensive Exam
exams.goal: Verify the learner's ability to apply Kantian formulas to maxims, distinguish between various types of rights, and compare major theories of distributive justice (Rawls vs. Nozick).
sections: This exam covers the application of the Categorical Imperative to moral maxims, the analysis of rights conflicts using the distinction between positive and negative rights, and the critical evaluation of social justice frameworks through the 'Original Position' and 'Entitlement Theory'.
successCriteria: Correctly identify the categorical imperative formulations in given scenarios.
Accurately categorize a set of rights as positive or negative.
Compare and contrast the distributive principles of Rawls and Nozick in a case study of tax policy.
Justify a moral position using at least one deontological argument.

units.title: Character and Care
units.description: Examine virtue-based approaches and the ethics of care, while delving into the psychological aspects of moral luck and responsibility.

lectures.title: Virtue Ethics
lectures.description: This lecture shifts the focus from 'what should I do' to 'what kind of person should I be' by exploring the classical Aristotelian tradition of moral character.

sessions.title: Aristotle and Flourishing
sessions.description: This session introduces the concept of Eudaimonia, often translated as flourishing or well-being, as the ultimate end of human action. You will learn to distinguish between instrumental goals and the final good of human life, helping you understand the teleological foundation of virtue ethics where morality is tied to fulfilling our human function.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by drawing a sharp contrast between the 'Action-Based' ethics studied in previous units (like Deontology or Utilitarianism) and the 'Character-Based' approach of Virtue Ethics. Use the whiteboard to sketch a simple diagram: on one side, an action being weighed by a rule; on the other, a person being shaped by their choices. Explain that for Aristotle, the central question isn't 'What should I do?' but 'What kind of person should I be?' This shift is crucial because it moves morality from a series of external checkboxes to an internal state of being. Introduce the term 'Teleology' by drawing an arrow pointing toward a target; explain that just as a knife has a purpose (cutting) and a seed has an end-state (a tree), human life is also directed toward a final 'telos' or end.

Introduce 'Eudaimonia' as that ultimate end. It is vital to preempt the common misunderstanding that Eudaimonia is simply 'happiness' in the modern, emotional sense. On the whiteboard, list 'Happiness' next to 'Flourishing' and cross out the former. Explain that while a feeling of pleasure is fleeting and passive, flourishing is an active state of excellence—like a musician playing at their peak or a plant thriving in perfect soil. Use a life scenario comparison: someone winning the lottery and sitting on a beach (pleasure/passive) versus someone dedicating years to mastering a craft and contributing to their community (Eudaimonia/active). This distinction reveals that morality is not a constraint on our happiness, but the very mechanism for achieving our highest potential.

Transition to the 'Function Argument' to explain why reason is the key to this flourishing. Ask the hypothetical: what makes a human being unique compared to a toaster, a horse, or a stone? Draw a hierarchy of souls on the board: Nutritive (plants), Sensitive (animals), and Rational (humans). Because reason is our unique function, flourishing for a human must involve the 'active life of the element that has a rational principle.' A 'good' human is one who performs this function well. Address the potential misconception that this is purely cold logic; explain that for Aristotle, using reason means harmonizing our emotions and desires with our understanding of what is right, rather than just solving math problems.

Conclude by framing the practice tasks as a diagnostic for internalizing this teleological view. In the first task, have the learner categorize scenarios—like the difference between 'binge-watching a show' and 'learning a difficult language'—to see if they can spot where short-term pleasure lacks the 'activity of soul' required for Eudaimonia. In the second task, push them to defend the 'function of man' argument. The goal here is for the learner to see that if we don't have a specific function or purpose, then 'ethics' becomes arbitrary. By grounding ethics in our nature as rational beings, Aristotle provides a foundational 'why' for being good that transcends mere social rules.

tasks: Identify the difference between 'pleasure' and 'Eudaimonia' in a series of life scenarios.
Explain why Aristotle believes the 'function of man' must involve reason.

sessions.title: The Virtues
sessions.description: This session explores the nature of moral virtues as stable dispositions or habits of character. You will learn the Doctrine of the Mean, which identifies virtue as the balance between the extremes of excess and deficiency, allowing you to map specific character traits like courage or temperance onto a spectrum of behavior.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by transitioning from the abstract concept of 'flourishing' to the concrete reality of human character. Use the whiteboard to define a 'virtue' not as a one-off good deed, but as a 'hexis'—a stable, ingrained disposition. It’s vital to explain that for Aristotle, being a good person isn't about following a checklist of rules, but about developing a reliable internal compass. Visualize this by drawing a person's character as a 'muscle' that has been trained over time to react instinctively to moral challenges. This reframing is essential because it moves the learner away from the 'calculating' mindset of Utilitarianism or the 'duty' mindset of Kant, focusing instead on the internal state of the agent.

Introduce the core framework of the session: The Doctrine of the Mean. Draw a horizontal line on the board. Explain that every virtue sits at a 'Golden Mean' between two extremes of vice—one of deficiency and one of excess. Use the classic example of 'Courage' to anchor this. On one end, there is 'Cowardice' (too much fear, not enough action); on the other, there is 'Rashness' (not enough fear, reckless action). Emphasize that the Mean is not a bland 'average' or a compromise, but a point of excellence. A common pitfall for students is thinking the Mean is 'moderate' in a way that lacks passion; clarify that excellence means feeling the right emotion, to the right degree, at the right time.

Deepen the application by moving to the virtue of 'Honesty' or 'Truthfulness.' Challenge the learner to identify the extremes themselves. They should arrive at 'Understatement/Self-deprecation' as the deficiency and 'Boastfulness' as the excess. Use this moment to introduce a crucial nuance: the Mean is relative to us. On the whiteboard, illustrate this with a metaphor of food portions—the 'mean' amount of food for a world-class athlete is vastly different from the 'mean' for a sedentary office worker. Similarly, the 'courageous' action for a trained soldier differs from that of a civilian. This prevents the misconception that Virtue Ethics is a 'one-size-fits-all' rigid system and introduces the idea of situational sensitivity.

Conclude the session by addressing the 'Precision' of the Mean. Explain that finding the Mean is difficult, which is why being good is rare and praiseworthy. Draw a target on the board, showing that there are many ways to miss the bullseye (the vices) but only one way to hit it (the virtue). This prepares the learner for the next session on Practical Wisdom by posing a problem: if the Mean isn't a mathematical midpoint, how do we actually find it? This cliffhanger ensures they understand that while the 'spectrum' model is a helpful tool for mapping character, the actual 'judgment' of where to stand on that spectrum requires a different kind of intellectual skill.

tasks: For the virtue of 'Honesty', identify the corresponding vices of excess and deficiency.
Discuss whether the 'Mean' is the same for every person in every situation.

sessions.title: Practical Wisdom
sessions.description: This session examines Phronesis, or practical wisdom, which is the intellectual virtue required to apply general moral principles to specific, messy situations. You will understand why rules alone are insufficient for moral life and how experience develops the 'moral eye' needed to perceive the right course of action in complex cases.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the assumption that ethics is a set of 'if-then' rules. In previous units, we looked at formulas like the Categorical Imperative or Utility calculations. This session introduces 'Phronesis', or Practical Wisdom, as the engine that drives virtue ethics. The core problem to present is the 'clash of virtues': what happens when being honest would also mean being unkind? Use the whiteboard to draw a scale that isn't just about 'Mean' and 'Excess' for one virtue, but a messy intersection where multiple virtues overlap. Explain that Phronesis is not a scientific formula but a 'moral eye'—the ability to perceive which virtue takes precedence in a specific, unique context.

Transition into the distinction between 'Natural Virtue' and 'Full Virtue' by using the example of a well-meaning child. A child might have a natural inclination to be brave or generous, but they lack the life experience to know *when* or *how* to exercise those traits effectively. On the whiteboard, contrast 'Impulse' with 'Deliberation.' Explain that Phronesis is an intellectual virtue, not a moral one; it is the cognitive skill of discernment. A common pitfall for students is thinking Phronesis is just 'common sense.' Clarify that it is actually a highly developed expert sensitivity, similar to how a master chef knows exactly when a dish needs more salt without measuring it—they just 'see' the requirement of the situation.

Introduce a complex case study to ground the theory. For instance, a friend asks for your honest opinion on their mediocre art project right before a major gallery opening. On the whiteboard, map out the competing demands: the virtue of Truthfulness, the virtue of Loyalty, and the virtue of Encouragement. Ask the learner to identify which path 'Practical Wisdom' would suggest. The goal of this exercise is to reveal that Phronesis doesn't find a middle ground between truth and lies, but rather finds the 'right' way to speak the truth—perhaps focusing on potential rather than failure—that serves the higher goal of 'Eudaimonia' for the friend. This demonstrates that moral life requires situational sensitivity, not just rigid adherence to a list of traits.

Conclude by addressing the 'Uncodifiability Thesis'—the idea that the right thing to do cannot be captured in a manual. This is why Aristotle emphasizes that we must look to the 'Phronimos' (the person of practical wisdom) as our benchmark. Use the whiteboard to illustrate a feedback loop: experience leads to better perception, better perception leads to better action, and better action builds a more refined 'moral eye.' This prepares the student for the final session on Moral Development by showing that we aren't born with this wisdom; we cultivate it through a lifetime of navigating the messy, unscripted reality of human relationships.

tasks: Analyze a case study where two virtues (e.g., kindness and truthfulness) conflict, and describe how practical wisdom resolves it.
Explain why a child can have 'natural virtue' but not 'practical wisdom'.

sessions.title: Moral Development
sessions.description: This session focuses on the process of habituation and how character is built through repeated action. You will learn that moral excellence is not an innate gift but a result of practice and social environment, providing you with a framework for understanding personal growth and the importance of role models in ethical education.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing a fundamental tension in Aristotle’s Ethics: the transition from 'knowing' to 'being.' After discussing the Doctrine of the Mean and Practical Wisdom, students often assume that moral life is a series of intellectual calculations. This session corrects that misconception by establishing that moral excellence is a craft (techne) acquired through habituation (ethismos). On the whiteboard, I will contrast 'innate traits' with 'acquired dispositions.' The goal is to show that while we are born with the capacity to receive virtue, we are not born virtuous. Like a musician who becomes a musician by playing an instrument, we become just by doing just acts and temperate by doing temperate acts.

I will then introduce the 'Paradox of Habituation' to spark critical thinking. The paradox is this: how can we perform virtuous acts to become virtuous if we aren't virtuous yet? To resolve this, I will draw a distinction between 'acts that happen to be virtuous' (done by chance or following orders) and 'acts done virtuously.' I'll use the analogy of learning a language; initially, a student repeats sounds without understanding the grammar, but through that mechanical repetition, they eventually internalize the structure and become a fluent speaker. This helps the learner understand that the 'fake it till you make it' phase is a necessary precursor to genuine moral character.

Next, the lecture shifts to the role of the social environment and 'Moral Exemplars.' Since virtue requires practice, the 'gym' for this practice is our community. I will visualize on the board how our circle of influence—parents, mentors, and peers—provides the initial 'scripts' for our behavior. This is where we discuss the importance of role models. Instead of following a list of rules, we look to a person of practical wisdom (the Phronimos) and ask, 'How would they react in this situation?' This moves the student away from abstract theory and toward observational learning. I'll caution against the misconception that this is mere 'blind imitation'; the goal is to observe the exemplar's judgment so we can eventually develop our own.

To wrap up, I will lead the learner through a reflective exercise on the 'viscosity' of habits. We will analyze a personal habit—perhaps a professional one like checking emails impulsively or a social one like interrupting others—to see how repetition creates a 'path of least resistance' in the brain. This illustrates Aristotle's point that once a character is formed, it becomes extremely difficult to act against it. This underscores the stakes of the session: we are currently building the person we will be tomorrow. The final discussion will critique the 'intellectualist' fallacy—the idea that reading a book on ethics makes one a better person—by arguing that without the 'training of the gut' through action, ethical knowledge remains a hollow theory.

tasks: Reflect on a personal habit and trace how it was formed through repetition.
Critique the idea that we can become 'virtuous' just by reading books about ethics.

lectures.title: Care and Relationships
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the Ethics of Care, a feminist-inspired framework that prioritizes relationality, empathy, and the specific needs of individuals over abstract universal rules.

sessions.title: The Ethics of Care
sessions.description: This session introduces the core tenets of Care Ethics as developed by thinkers like Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings. You will learn how this approach differs from 'justice-based' ethics by emphasizing emotional responsiveness and the fundamental interconnectedness of persons, which serves as a necessary corrective to the atomistic individualism of traditional theories.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the traditional 'justice' perspective that has dominated the course so far. On the whiteboard, draw a line down the center. On one side, write 'The Voice of Justice.' This represents the Enlightenment focus on autonomy, impartial rules, and abstract rights seen in Kant and Utilitarianism. Explain that while these theories are powerful, they often assume a 'self-made man' archetype—an atomistic individual who is fully independent and rational. The 'Ethics of Care' begins by pointing out the biological and social falsity of this assumption: none of us survived infancy or will survive old age without intense, non-contractual care from others.

Introduce Carol Gilligan’s work as a corrective to psychological models of moral development. Explain the core shift from asking 'What is the fair rule for everyone?' to 'How do I respond to the specific needs of this person in this relationship?' Use the whiteboard to contrast these two questions. It is crucial to emphasize that Care Ethics is not merely about 'being nice' or 'empathy' as a vague feeling; it is a rigorous moral framework centered on 'relationality.' The most important idea here is that our moral obligations are often unchosen—we find ourselves in relationships of dependency (like a child to a parent) that demand a response, regardless of any social contract or universal law.

Transition to the mechanics of care as defined by Nel Noddings. Distinguish between 'caring-about' (a general concern for suffering) and 'caring-for' (the actual, labor-intensive practice of meeting a specific person's needs). On the board, visualize this as a circle of concern where the intensity of moral obligation increases with the proximity and vulnerability of the other person. This is where you address the common misconception that Care Ethics is 'irrational' or purely emotional. Explain that it requires 'engrossment'—a deep, cognitive focus on the other person's reality—and 'motive displacement,' where the caregiver’s goals temporarily take a backseat to the needs of the cared-for.

Lead the learner into the first practice task by presenting a dilemma where a strict rule (justice) conflicts with a relationship (care), such as a manager deciding whether to fire an employee who is underperforming due to a family crisis. Have the learner articulate the 'Voice of Justice' (efficiency, fairness to other employees, contracts) versus the 'Voice of Care' (support for the individual, long-term loyalty, recognizing the crisis). This exercise is designed to reveal if the learner can see care as a distinct moral logic rather than just an exception to a rule.

Conclude by explicitly mapping the differences between Kantian 'Duty' and 'Care.' While Kantian duty is grounded in a universal law that must be applied regardless of the person, Care is grounded in the maintenance of the connection itself. Help the learner see that while Kant treats people as 'ends in themselves' to avoid exploitation, Care Ethics treats them as 'particular individuals' to ensure they are sustained. This sets the stage for the next session on partiality, as the learner begins to see why treating everyone exactly the same might actually be a moral failure in the context of intimate relationships.

tasks: Compare the 'Voice of Justice' with the 'Voice of Care' in response to a moral dilemma.
List three key differences between Kantian duty and the duty to care.

sessions.title: Partiality and Special Obligations
sessions.description: This session challenges the utilitarian demand for impartiality by exploring special obligations we owe to those close to us. You will learn why it might be morally permissible—or even required—to prioritize your own family or friends over strangers, helping you navigate the tension between universal human rights and personal loyalties.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a sharp contrast on the whiteboard between the 'Impartial Spectator' of Utilitarianism and the 'Embedded Self' of Care Ethics. Begin by visually representing the classical Utilitarian position: a series of identical circles representing individuals, where the moral agent stands at an equal distance from each. Explain that for thinkers like Peter Singer, every '1' unit of suffering is equal regardless of whose it is. This sets the stage for the core conflict of the session: the tension between our abstract duty to humanity and our felt duty to those we love. By framing the 'God’s eye view' as the standard we are about to challenge, you prepare the learner to see partiality not as a moral failing, but as a potential moral requirement.

Introduce the 'Burning House' or 'Drowning Stranger' thought experiment to ground the theoretical tension. Draw two paths from a central figure (the agent): one leading to a parent or child, and the other to a brilliant stranger who might cure cancer.
